full_text_sections.conclusion: 3.ConclusionThis work demonstrates primer‐programmed amplicon encoding as a probe‐free strategy for multiplex nucleic acid identification by coupling one‐pot RPA with solid‐state nanopore readout and deep learning‐based decoding. Primer‐programmed amplicons with predefined product lengths enable direct electrical identification of Mpox, Cowpox, Vaccinia, and human RNase P without reliance on target‐specific reporter probes or multichannel optical detection, while an assay‐specific nanopore operating window of 6.3–9.1 nm supports stable signal acquisition. Multidimensional feature‐based classification using a DNN achieves high event‐level performance, with true positive rates of 94.7%–98.9% and strong precision, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 scores. Aggregation of event‐level predictions using an NTC‐referenced decision rule enables robust sample‐level calling, with qualitative calls matching PCR‐defined target compositions across the 9 benchmark mixtures tested and reproducible performance across independent nanopores, while blinded testing demonstrates sensitivities of 93.3%–100% and specificities of 93.9%–100%. This work demonstrates a multiplexing architecture in which target identity is encoded in the physical properties of the amplification product itself rather than in an external reporter. The present four‐target synthetic system establishes the feasibility of the encoding and decoding framework but does not define the minimum resolvable amplicon‐length spacing or maximum multiplex capacity. Future scalability will depend on the usable amplicon‐length coding space, multiplex amplification robustness, and nanopore resolution, whereas clinical translation will require quantitative validation in representative biological matrices, broader concentration‐dependent testing, and systematic evaluation of target‐specific amplification efficiency. Improved translocation control and signal resolution may enable denser primer‐programmed amplicon encoding within the amplification‐compatible size range.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionMultiplexed NATs are central to infectious disease diagnosis. Many clinical syndromes can arise from pathogens with overlapping clinical presentations [1]. Respiratory infections [2, 3, 4], febrile illness [5, 6, 7], and rash syndromes [8] are common examples. Co‐infections further complicate diagnosis and clinical management [9]. Panel‐based molecular tests, therefore, provide clinically useful information from a single specimen [4]. Rapid multiplex detection can guide treatment decisions, reduce unnecessary antimicrobial use [10], and support outbreak surveillance [11]. Multiplexing is commonly implemented in two formats: multiple singleplex assays are run in parallel, or multiple targets are amplified within a single reaction. Parallel singleplex testing preserves assay simplicity but increases sample consumption, reagent use, and workflow burden [12]. In contrast, single‐reaction multiplex amplification allows pathogen targets and internal controls to be co‐amplified under shared conditions [13, 14, 15]. This integration reduces handling steps and improves assay efficiency [16]. As a result, single‐reaction multiplex assays are increasingly used in syndromic diagnostics.Despite these practical advantages, most multiplex NATs assign target identity through extrinsic encoding [17]. In quantitative PCR and digital PCR, sequence‐specific probes carry distinct fluorophores [18], and targets are distinguished through spectrally separated detection channels [15]. Other approaches extend multiplex capacity through fluorescence lifetime encoding [19], temperature‐dependent signatures [20], or spatial barcoding on arrays [21] and bead libraries [22, 23]. Although effective, these strategies share a common feature: target identity is encoded by external reporters rather than by the amplification product itself. Practical multiplex performance is therefore shaped by the number of distinguishable reporters, spectral crosstalk, calibration requirements, and the availability of distinct optical detection channels [15, 24, 25]. Increasing the multiplex level also introduces biochemical constraints within the amplification reaction. As the number of primers and probes increases, the number of possible oligonucleotide interactions also increases, which can introduce amplification bias [26, 27]. These side reactions consume reagents and reduce amplification efficiency [27]. Competition among targets can compress dynamic range and create target‐dependent sensitivity. These effects complicate assay optimization and make multiplex assay design increasingly difficult. Collectively, these limitations motivate reconsideration of how multiplex decoding can be implemented. Nucleic acid amplification generates discrete DNA molecules with defined sequence composition and length [28], and these unmodified molecular properties could provide target‐associated information directly. If amplification products can be measured at the single‐molecule level, the amplicon itself could serve as the identifier. In this case, multiplex decoding would then rely on molecular features rather than on designed reporter chemistry.Solid‐state nanopores provide a direct electrical interface for measuring properties of DNA molecules [29, 30, 31, 32]. Under an applied electric field, individual DNA strands translocate through a nanometer‐scale pore and generate transient ionic current blockades. The amplitude, duration, and waveform of each event reflect molecular size and conformation [33, 34]. Nanopore sensors can therefore detect DNA fragments at the single‐molecule level and distinguish molecules with different lengths [35]. Prior studies have also used nanopores for molecular identification and multiplex readout through designed DNA carriers [36], DNA nanoarray barcodes [37], site‐specific protein barcodes [38], and related engineered barcode architectures. These studies demonstrate the capability of nanopores to decode molecular identity, but the target‐identifying information is typically introduced through external carrier structures, affinity‐mediated binding, conjugation chemistry, barcode‐forming reagents, or engineered molecular labels rather than being inherent to the amplification product itself. Such strategies may also require additional assembly or binding steps, and incomplete target‐carrier association can reduce the fraction of informative sensing events. By contrast, primer‐programmed unmodified amplicon encoding does not require target‐specific reporter probes, engineered carriers, affinity labels, or post‐amplification barcode‐forming chemistry for target identification. Target identity is encoded at the primer‐design stage through the length of the amplification product itself, which is also the nanopore‐sensed identifier.A complementary approach is therefore to use the unmodified amplification product itself as the identifier, so that the same molecule generated by amplification also provides the physical feature used for decoding. This distinction is important because probe‐free multiplex amplicon decoding presents a more complex measurement problem than reading purified engineered barcodes or well‐defined analytes. Recent studies have coupled nanopores with nucleic acid amplification to electronically detect amplification products [30, 32, 39]. Computational analysis using machine learning (ML) can further improve the interpretation of nanopore signals by integrating multidimensional signal features [34, 40, 41]. This is useful because conventional threshold‐based analysis often depends on manually selected cutoffs for individual descriptors, such as blockade amplitude, dwell time, or event charge deficit. These cutoffs can be sensitive to pore geometry, event frequency, baseline noise, and experimental conditions. In contrast, a trained classifier can combine multiple event descriptors within a consistent decision framework, reducing reliance on manually chosen single‐parameter thresholds. Probe‐free multiplex decoding nevertheless remains challenging [42]. Single‐reaction multiplex amplification can produce complex mixtures containing both intended amplicons and nonspecific products [27]. Nanopore signals may also vary across pores and fluctuate over time [43, 44]. These sources of heterogeneity limit simple threshold‐based decoding. An analytical framework must therefore convert large numbers of stochastic single‐molecule events into reliable sample‐level calls anchored to appropriate negative controls.Here, we present a probe‐free multiplex decoding framework based on primer‐programmed unmodified amplicon encoding and nanopore readout. As a proof‐of‐concept model implementation of this strategy, we used single‐reaction RPA and designed primer sets that generate amplicons with separable lengths. Unmodified amplicon length generated by pre‐programmed primers thus serves as an encoding dimension. Mixed amplification products were analyzed using glass nanopores, and individual translocation events were classified using multidimensional nanopore signal features with a DNN model. Event‐level predictions were then aggregated into sample‐level calls using thresholds defined relative to the no‐template control (NTC). Using this framework, we demonstrate four‐target multiplex detection within a single reaction and reproducible sample‐level decoding across independent nanopores. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a novel method for multiplex nucleic acid testing that eliminates the need for target-specific reporters or probes, addressing the challenge of distinguishing multiple co-amplified targets within a single reaction.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a proof-of-concept implementation using recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) to generate amplicons from Monkeypox (Mpox), Cowpox, Vaccinia, and human RNase P. A held-out validation dataset of 23 samples and a separate blinded cohort of 62 samples were used for model evaluation.
analysis.methods: The method utilized primer-programmed amplicon design to generate target-associated amplicons with predefined lengths, which were then analyzed using glass nanopores. Individual translocation events were classified by a deep neural network (DNN) based on a six-dimensional feature set derived from nanopore recordings. Primer quality was assessed using established guidelines and open-source software.
analysis.main_results: Event-level decoding achieved >95% accuracy, >94.7% sensitivity, and >98.3% specificity. Sample-level calls showed >93.3% sensitivity and >93.9% specificity in blinded samples, with qualitative calls matching polymerase chain reaction (PCR) results across 9 PCR-benchmarked samples.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these results as demonstrating a probe-free multiplexing architecture that uses primer-defined amplicon design and deep learning decoding, offering new opportunities for all-electrical nucleic acid testing without the need for target-specific reporter chemistry.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide a novel approach for multiplex nucleic acid testing that could improve the efficiency and accuracy of diagnostic methods for Mpox and related viruses, supporting better surveillance and rapid identification in clinical and public health settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's results are based on a limited number of samples and nanopores, and the model's performance was evaluated on a blinded cohort not used for training. The evidence is moderate, as the methodology is promising but requires further validation in larger and more diverse datasets.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a novel probe-free, primer-programmed multiplex nucleic acid testing method using glass nanopore sensing and deep learning decoding. The approach eliminates the need for target-specific reporters by generating amplicons with predefined lengths through primer design. In a proof-of-concept implementation, RPA was used to amplify four targets: Monkeypox (Mpox), Cowpox, Vaccinia, and human RNase P. The resulting amplicons were analyzed using nanopores, and individual translocation events were classified by a deep neural network (DNN) based on a six-dimensional feature set. The method achieved high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity at both event and sample levels, with results matching PCR benchmarks. The study used a held-out validation dataset of 23 samples and a separate blinded cohort of 62 samples for evaluation, ensuring independence from the training data. The findings suggest a promising new architecture for all-electrical multiplex testing, potentially improving diagnostic efficiency for Mpox and related viruses. However, the evidence is moderate due to the limited sample size and the need for further validation in diverse settings.

WATCHREAD MORE NEWS Health District reports first clade I mpox case in Clark County resident by Matthew Seeman Tue, October 20, 2026 at 9:08 AM Updated Tue, October 20, 2026 at 2:53 PM 3VIEW ALL PHOTOS FILE: Southern Nevada Health District (KSNV) 0Comment Share topics: Mpox Clade I Clark County Southern Nevada Health District JYNNEOS Clade II Vaccination Public health LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Health officials are reporting the first case of clade I mpox in a Clark County resident. The Southern Nevada Health District (SNHD) says the individual has no reported travel exposure. Separately, there have been 11 confirmed cases of clade II mpox in Clark County since this August, marking a recent increase in cases. "This first clade I case and the recent increase in clade II cases are reminders that mpox continues to circulate in our community," Dr. Cassius Lockett, SNHD's District Health Officer, said in a statement. "We encourage people at risk to get vaccinated and anyone who may have been exposed to seek guidance promptly. Recognizing symptoms and avoiding close contact when sick can also help prevent further spread." Clade I and clade II are two types of viruses that cause mpox. Clade II caused the global outbreak that began in 2022 and continues to circulate at low levels in the U.S. Powered By 10 Sec Teen critically injured in Henderson e-scooter crash dies, police continue investigation Next Stay A large clade I outbreak spread widely in Central and Eastern Africa in 2024, with cases later identified in other countries, including the U.S. The JYNNEOS vaccine is expected to protect against both types, and the SNHD offers mpox vaccination at its immunization clinics. Mpox spreads primarily through close, sustained physical contact, including sexual or intimate contact. It can spread through direct contact with a person's rash, sores, scabs or bodily fluids, including during kissing or oral, anal or vaginal sex. It can also spread through contact with contaminated items, such as clothing, bedding or towels, and during pregnancy or childbirth. Symptoms usually begin within three weeks of exposure, and illness usually lasts two to four weeks. A rash may appear as bumps or blisters on or near the genitals or anus, or on other areas such as the hands, feet, chest, face or mouth. Other symptoms can include fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, muscle aches and fatigue. Some people develop a rash without other symptoms. People with suspected or confirmed mpox should take the following steps to prevent spreading the illness: Stay home and avoid close contact with others, including people and pets in the same household. Avoid sexual contact, kissing and other close physical contact. If being around others is unavoidable, wear a well-fitting mask and completely cover rashes and sores with clothing or bandages. Avoid sharing clothing, bedding, towels and other personal items. Wash hands frequently with soap and water, especially after touching the rash. Use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer if soap and water are unavailable. This marks a new development in the mpox situation in the area. The individual has no reported travel exposure, and the SNHD is emphasizing the importance of vaccination and prompt guidance for those exposed. Since August 2026, there have been 11 confirmed cases of clade II mpox in Clark County, indicating a recent increase in cases. The health district is reminding the public that mpox continues to circulate in the community and urging people at risk to get vaccinated. The JYNNEOS vaccine is expected to protect against both clade I and II mpox. The SNHD is offering mpox vaccination at its immunization clinics. The response includes public health guidance and ongoing investigation into the spread of the virus.

The Southern Nevada Health District confirmed the case this week, marking the first time the clade I strain has turned up in a local resident without a clear travel link. The health district reported the case as part of a broader update on mpox activity in the Las Vegas area, according to KSNV. Since the virus was first detected locally in June 2022, Clark County has logged 365 total mpox cases, according to the Southern Nevada Health District. The district also noted that 11 confirmed clade II cases have surfaced locally between August and October 2026, a sign of increased virus activity heading into the clade I discovery. No Clear Source of Exposure SNHD has said the individual diagnosed with clade I mpox has no reported travel exposure, leaving the source of transmission unclear. Dr. Cassius Lockett, the district's health officer, said mpox continues to circulate in the community and encouraged people at risk to get vaccinated and those potentially exposed to seek guidance promptly. Lockett also said that recognizing symptoms early and avoiding close contact with others while sick can help prevent further spread, per the same report from the health district. Clade I and clade II are the two viral types behind mpox illness. Clade II caused the global outbreak that began in 2022 and continues to circulate at low levels across the U.S., while clade I spread widely across Central and Eastern Africa in 2024 before cases began appearing in other countries, including the United States, the health district's report notes. Why Clade I Draws Closer Scrutiny The heightened concern around clade I stems from its track record overseas. According to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, clade I mpox has historically produced case fatality rates between 1% and 10% in African outbreaks, compared with less than 1% to 4% for clade II. The World Health Organization declared clade I a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in August 2024 amid a rapid surge of the clade Ib strain across Central and Eastern Africa, its second such mpox declaration. Clade I's arrival in the U.S. has followed a steady progression. The first known American case was confirmed in a traveler returning from Eastern Africa to California in November 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Nearly a year later, in October 2025, Long Beach, California recorded the nation's first locally acquired clade I case in a patient with no travel history, as reported by CIDRAP. Similar travel-linked and non-travel cases have since surfaced elsewhere, including in Arizona and San Diego County. Vaccine and Exposure Guidance Health officials emphasize that the Jynneos vaccine is expected to protect against both clade I and clade II mpox, and SNHD continues to offer it at its immunization clinics. By August 2024, clinics affiliated with the health district had already administered more than 11,740 doses across Clark County, reflecting the scale of earlier vaccination efforts following the 2022 outbreak. The standard Jynneos regimen for adults 18 and older requires two doses spaced four weeks, or 28 days, apart to achieve full protection, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For those who may have been exposed, the agency says post-exposure vaccination works best within four days of exposure, though getting the shot between four and 14 days afterward can still reduce how severe symptoms become. Anyone potentially exposed should monitor for symptoms for 21 days following their last contact, per SNHD guidance. How Mpox Spreads and What Symptoms Look Like Mpox spreads primarily through close, sustained physical contact, including direct contact with rash, sores, scabs or bodily fluids, as well as through kissing or oral, anal or vaginal sex. It can also spread through contaminated clothing, bedding or towels, and through pregnancy or childbirth. Symptoms usually begin within three weeks of exposure and the illness typically lasts two to four weeks, with a rash that may appear on or near the genitals or anus, or on the hands, feet, chest, face or mouth. Other symptoms can include fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, muscle aches and fatigue, though some people develop only a rash without any other symptoms. Anyone with suspected or confirmed mpox is advised to stay home and avoid close contact with others, including household members and pets, and to avoid sexual contact, kissing and other close physical contact. If contact with others is unavoidable, health officials recommend wearing a well-fitting mask and completely covering rashes and sores with clothing or bandages. People with mpox should also avoid sharing clothing, bedding, towels and other personal items, and should wash their hands frequently with soap and water, especially after touching the rash, using an alcohol-based hand sanitizer when soap and water aren't available. Isolation should continue until all sores have healed, scabs have fallen off and a fresh layer of skin has formed, per the health district's guidance. Since the virus was first detected locally in June 2022, Clark County has logged 365 total mpox cases, according to the Southern Nevada Health District. The district also noted that 11 confirmed clade II cases have surfaced locally between August and October 2026, a sign of increased virus activity heading into the clade I discovery. No Clear Source of Exposure SNHD has said the individual diagnosed with clade I mpox has no reported travel exposure, leaving the source of transmission unclear. Dr. Cassius Lockett, the district's health officer, said mpox continues to circulate in the community and encouraged people at risk to get vaccinated and those potentially exposed to seek guidance promptly. Lockett also said that recognizing symptoms early and avoiding close contact with others while sick can help prevent further spread, per the same report from the health district. Clade I and clade II are the two viral types behind mpox illness. Clade II caused the global outbreak that began in 2022 and continues to circulate at low levels across the U.S., while clade I spread widely across Central and Eastern Africa in 2024 before cases began appearing in other countries, including the United States, the health district's report notes. Why Clade I Draws Closer Scrutiny The heightened concern around clade I stems from its track record overseas. According to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, clade I mpox has historically produced case fatality rates between 1% and 10% in African outbreaks, compared with less than 1% to 4% for clade II. The World Health Organization declared clade I a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in August 2024 amid a rapid surge of the clade Ib strain across Central and Eastern Africa, its second such mpox declaration. Clade I's arrival in the U.S. has followed a steady progression. The first known American case was confirmed in a traveler returning from Eastern Africa to California in November 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Nearly a year later, in October 2025, Long Beach, California recorded the nation's first locally acquired clade I case in a patient with no travel history, as reported by CIDRAP. Similar travel-linked and non-travel cases have since surfaced elsewhere, including in Arizona and San Diego County. Vaccine and Exposure Guidance Health officials emphasize that the Jynneos vaccine is expected to protect against both clade I and clade II mpox, and SNHD continues to offer it at its immunization clinics. By August 2024, clinics affiliated with the health district had already administered more than 11,740 doses across Clark County, reflecting the scale of earlier vaccination efforts following the 2022 outbreak. The standard Jynneos regimen for adults 18 and older requires two doses spaced four weeks, or 28 days, apart to achieve full protection, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For those who may have been exposed, the agency says post-exposure vaccination works best within four days of exposure, though getting the shot between four and 14 days afterward can still reduce how severe symptoms become. Anyone potentially exposed should monitor for symptoms for 21 days following their last contact, per SNHD guidance. How Mpox Spreads and What Symptoms Look Like Mpox spreads primarily through close, sustained physical contact, including direct contact with rash, sores, scabs or bodily fluids, as well as through kissing or oral, anal or vaginal sex. It can also spread through contaminated clothing, bedding or towels, and through pregnancy or childbirth. Symptoms usually begin within three weeks of exposure and the illness typically lasts two to four weeks, with a rash that may appear on or near the genitals or anus, or on the hands, feet, chest, face or mouth. Other symptoms can include fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, muscle aches and fatigue, though some people develop only a rash without any other symptoms. Anyone with suspected or confirmed mpox is advised to stay home and avoid close contact with others, including household members and pets, and to avoid sexual contact, kissing and other close physical contact. If contact with others is unavoidable, health officials recommend wearing a well-fitting mask and completely covering rashes and sores with clothing or bandages. People with mpox should also avoid sharing clothing, bedding, towels and other personal items, and should wash their hands frequently with soap and water, especially after touching the rash, using an alcohol-based hand sanitizer when soap and water aren't available. Isolation should continue until all sores have healed, scabs have fallen off and a fresh layer of skin has formed, per the health district's guidance. By Rachel Zalucki Published: Oct. 20, 2026 at 3:57 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google LAS VEGAS (FOX5) — The Southern Nevada Health District announced Tuesday the first confirmed case of Clade I Mpox in a Clark County resident. The individual has no reported travel exposure, according to the Health District. MORE ON FOX5: More than 37,000 vote in first three days of early voting in Clark County The Health District has also reported 11 confirmed cases of Clade II Mpox since August 2026, marking a recent increase in cases. Since the first mpox case was reported in Clark County in June 2022, the Health District has reported 365 cases. “This first clade I case and the recent increase in clade II cases are reminders that mpox continues to circulate in our community,” said Dr. Cassius Lockett, District Health Officer for the Health District. “We encourage people at risk to get vaccinated and anyone who may have been exposed to seek guidance promptly. Recognizing symptoms and avoiding close contact when sick can also help prevent further spread.” About the two virus types Mpox is caused by two types of virus, known as clade I and clade II, according to the Health District. Clade II caused the global outbreak that began in 2022 and continues to circulate at low levels in the United States. A Clade I outbreak spread widely in Central and Eastern Africa in 2024, with cases subsequently identified in other countries, including the United States. Both types can be prevented in the same ways, and the JYNNEOS vaccine is expected to protect against both, the Health District said. Mpox spreads primarily through close, sustained physical contact, including sexual or intimate contact, according to the Health District. It can spread through direct contact with a person’s rash, sores, scabs or bodily fluids, including during kissing or oral, anal or vaginal sex. It can also spread through contact with contaminated items, such as clothing, bedding or towels, and during pregnancy or childbirth. Symptoms typically begin within three weeks of exposure, and illness usually lasts two to four weeks, the Health District said. A rash may appear as bumps or blisters on or near the genitals or anus, or on other areas such as the hands, feet, chest, face or mouth. Other symptoms can include fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, muscle aches and fatigue. Some people develop a rash without other symptoms. Anyone who develops a new or unexplained rash or other symptoms consistent with mpox should avoid close contact with others and contact a health care provider, according to the Health District. People are advised to call ahead before visiting a health care facility to let staff know about possible mpox symptoms. The Health District offers mpox vaccination for eligible people ages 18 and older at its immunization clinics. The vaccine is given in two doses, four weeks apart. By Rachel Zalucki Published: Oct. 20, 2026 at 3:57 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google LAS VEGAS (FOX5) — The Southern Nevada Health District announced Tuesday the first confirmed case of Clade I Mpox in a Clark County resident. The individual has no reported travel exposure, according to the Health District. MORE ON FOX5: More than 37,000 vote in first three days of early voting in Clark County The Health District has also reported 11 confirmed cases of Clade II Mpox since August 2026, marking a recent increase in cases. Since the first mpox case was reported in Clark County in June 2022, the Health District has reported 365 cases. “This first clade I case and the recent increase in clade II cases are reminders that mpox continues to circulate in our community,” said Dr. Cassius Lockett, District Health Officer for the Health District. “We encourage people at risk to get vaccinated and anyone who may have been exposed to seek guidance promptly. Recognizing symptoms and avoiding close contact when sick can also help prevent further spread.” About the two virus types Mpox is caused by two types of virus, known as clade I and clade II, according to the Health District. Clade II caused the global outbreak that began in 2022 and continues to circulate at low levels in the United States. A Clade I outbreak spread widely in Central and Eastern Africa in 2024, with cases subsequently identified in other countries, including the United States. Both types can be prevented in the same ways, and the JYNNEOS vaccine is expected to protect against both, the Health District said. Mpox spreads primarily through close, sustained physical contact, including sexual or intimate contact, according to the Health District. It can spread through direct contact with a person’s rash, sores, scabs or bodily fluids, including during kissing or oral, anal or vaginal sex. It can also spread through contact with contaminated items, such as clothing, bedding or towels, and during pregnancy or childbirth. Symptoms typically begin within three weeks of exposure, and illness usually lasts two to four weeks, the Health District said. A rash may appear as bumps or blisters on or near the genitals or anus, or on other areas such as the hands, feet, chest, face or mouth. Other symptoms can include fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, muscle aches and fatigue. Some people develop a rash without other symptoms. Anyone who develops a new or unexplained rash or other symptoms consistent with mpox should avoid close contact with others and contact a health care provider, according to the Health District. People are advised to call ahead before visiting a health care facility to let staff know about possible mpox symptoms. The Health District offers mpox vaccination for eligible people ages 18 and older at its immunization clinics. The vaccine is given in two doses, four weeks apart. Appointments are available on the Southern Nevada Health District website. Copyright 2026 KVVU. All rights reserved. news.content: EPAPER LIVE TV DAWNNEWS URDU Images Herald Aurora CityFM89 Advertise Events Supplements Careers Obituaries Dawn E-Paper | October 26, 2026 Home Latest US-Iran War Pakistan Opinion Business Images Prism World Sport Breathe Magazines Tech Videos Popular Archive Flood Donations Home Latest US-Iran War Pakistan Opinion Business Images Prism World Sport Breathe Magazines Tech Videos Popular Archive Flood Donations Search Search Subscribe to notifications Get the latest news and updates from Dawn Not Now Allow Notifications Four Mpox cases detected in KP Ashfaq Yusufzai Published October 25, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 10:27am Email Story Your Name * Recipient Email * Send Email Cancel 0 A test tube labelled "Mpox virus positive" is held in this illustration taken August 20, 2024. — Reuters/File comments Join our Whatsapp Channel PESHAWAR: Authorities have detected four new Mpox cases, including a couple, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, revealing that none of them has a history of foreign travel. As health experts fear the risk of the local transmission of the virus, the health department has planned contact tracing and testing of the close relatives of the infected people, say officials. They said the Public Health Reference Laboratory at the Khyber Medical University, which tested samples for infectious diseases, received samples from suspected patients referred by the Khyber Teaching Hospital last week. They tested positive for Mpox on Saturday. Officials said one woman and three men were sent home to remain in isolation. Contact tracing, testing planned amid fears of virus’s local transmission They said two patients belonged to Nowshera, while the other two were from Peshawar and Mardan. According to a report prepared by the health department’s Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response System, the latest case detections have taken the province’s Mpox tally for the current year to 18. Of them, one lost his life, while 13 patients were recovered. Doctors called the situation alarming in light of the possibility of community transmission. Until now this year, the province has reported two Mpox cases in Swabi in Jan; four in Feb, including two in Buner and one each in Abbottabad and Lower Chitral; one in Peshawar in March; one in Karak in April; one in Upper Chitral in July; one in Mardan in Aug, and four in Sept, including three in Peshawar and one in Upper Dir. Doctors fear outbreaks and call for wider infection prevention measures along with the establishment of isolation rooms in hospitals to help prevent the spread of the disease. Health officials said the department had already issued guidelines to hospitals, especially those in affected districts, asking them to collect samples from suspected Mpox patients for laboratory confirmation to ensure strict surveillance through timely diagnosis. They said Mpox cases reported in the province previously were mainly linked to international travel, with patients contracting the infection abroad before entering the country. Officials said the province recorded its first Mpox case in 2023 when a resident working as a driver in Saudi Arabia tested positive for the disease after landing at the airport. Health experts called stronger preventive measures to contain possible local transmission of the disease. “We need to strengthen infection control measures and ensure that the reuse of syringes is stopped. More infections could be detected if screening is carried out in areas from where the latest cases have been reported,” an expert told Dawn. Dermatologists noted that the World Health Organisation declared Mpox a public health emergency of international concern on Aug 14, 2024, following an upsurge in cases amid the continuing threat posed by the infection. Prof Mehran Khan, associate professor and chairman of the dermatology department at Khyber Teaching Hospital, said the disease typically began with fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, swollen lymph nodes, chills and exhaustion. He said the rash evolved from macules (flat lesions) to papules (raised lesions), vesicles (fluid-filled lesions), pustules (pus-filled lesions) and finally crusts, while the lesions eventually fell off. “Mpox is transmittable through direct contact with blood, bodily fluids or cutaneous or mucosal lesions of infected patients and indirect contact through contaminated materials such as bedding,” he said. Doctors said the risk of infection could be reduced by preventing direct contact with affected people, wearing face masks and taking recommended precautionary steps. They also said in Pakistan, only Clade-I variant of Mpox virus was prevalent but it wasn’t threatening like Clade-II whose presence had so far not been reported in the country. Doctors said the province had recorded one death among Mpox patients though the deceased might have been a “co-morbid” Mpox patient. news.content: TODAY’S PAPER | October 26, 2026 | EPAPER ☰ Home Latest Pakistan Business World Sports Opinion Life & Style T-Magazine Blogs Tech Cartoon Home Sindh Tally hits 95 as two more mpox cases reported in Sindh Province reports 11 deaths from virus so far this year Our Correspondent October 23, 2026 1 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email The image shows Mpox micrograph in the background. PHOTO: PIXABAY KARACHI: Sindh has reported two more cases of monkeypox, or mpox, taking the total caseload recorded in the province this year to 95. The virus has claimed 11 lives so far. The latest cases involve 21-year-old Salman Ali and 23-year-old Ishrat Fatima, both of whom tested positive for the virus, according to a report by Dow University's provincial public health laboratory. Advertisement X Both patients are already receiving treatment at the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital, officials said. The emergence of additional cases has underscored the importance of continued surveillance and preventive measures to contain the spread of the virus. Of the 95 cases thus far, 71 were men, accounting for 75.27 per cent, while 24 were women. People aged 30 to 39 were the most affected age group, with 26 confirmed cases, while 23 children up to the age of nine also tested positive for mpox. April recorded the highest number of cases at 31, followed by September with 20, August 17, July seven, October six so far, March five, June four and May two. Experts said mpox is a viral disease that can spread through close physical or skin-to-skin contact with an infected person, as well as contact with lesions, bodily fluids or contaminated objects. Suspected patients should also limit close contact with others to reduce the risk of transmission, experts said. news.content: TODAY’S PAPER | October 26, 2026 | EPAPER ☰ Home Latest Pakistan Business World Sports Opinion Life & Style T-Magazine Blogs Tech Cartoon Home Pakistan Sindh reports two more monkeypox cases, tally rises to 98 Seven cases detected in a week; health dept steps up contact tracing and surveillance Our Correspondent October 24, 2026 1 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email Test tubes labelled 'Monkeypox virus positive' are seen in this illustration taken May 23, 2022. PHOTO: REUTERS KARACHI: The Sindh Health Department on Friday reported two more cases of monkeypox, or mpox, taking the provincial tally to 98, as the department stepped up surveillance, contact tracing and patient care following seven new infections in the past week. It said authorities are tracing and monitoring people who came into contact with infected patients to contain the spread of the virus. The department also directed public and private healthcare facilities to strictly implement infection prevention and control measures. Advertisements Video Player is loading. Advertisement X Read: Tally hits 95 as two more mpox cases reported in Sindh Citizens have also been advised to maintain proper hand hygiene and avoid direct contact with rashes, blisters and sores on suspected or confirmed patients. They have been cautioned against sharing personal items used by infected individuals, including towels, clothing and bedding. People developing unusual rashes or blisters have been urged to seek immediate medical attention and inform their doctors about any contact with a suspected mpox patient. The health department said mpox was a preventable and treatable public health concern, urging citizens to follow precautionary measures and rely on official sources for verified information rather than spreading unconfirmed reports. Sindh's mpox outbreak has intensified in recent months, with health authorities reporting a steady rise in infections across the province. Earlier this month, The Express Tribune reported 95 confirmed cases and 11 deaths, highlighting a growing need for stronger surveillance, early diagnosis and contact tracing. The outbreak has extended beyond imported infections, with cases reported among Karachi residents who had no history of foreign travel. In June, a 26-year-old security guard in Karachi had tested positive, taking the provincial tally to 37 at the time. Earlier reports also documented infections in Khairpur and Karachi, prompting authorities to establish isolation facilities and strengthen infection-control arrangements in hospitals. Health experts have warned that delayed diagnosis and stigma can discourage patients from seeking timely medical care, increasing the risk of further transmission. Mpox can spread through close physical contact with an infected person, contact with skin lesions and contaminated personal items. Symptoms can include fever, body aches, swollen lymph nodes, and unusual skin rashes or blisters. analysis.event: Sindh Health Department reported two additional monkeypox cases, raising the provincial tally to 98. The outbreak has intensified with cases reported among local residents.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 98 confirmed cases of monkeypox in Sindh, with a steady rise in infections. The health department emphasized the need for stronger surveillance, early diagnosis, and contact tracing to contain the spread.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Authorities are tracing and monitoring contacts of infected patients, implementing infection prevention and control measures in healthcare facilities, and advising citizens to maintain hygiene and avoid direct contact with rashes or blisters. The health department has also urged early testing and isolation of confirmed patients.

analysis.brief_en: The Sindh Health Department reported two additional monkeypox cases on October 24, 2026, bringing the provincial total to 98. This marks an intensification of the outbreak, with cases now being reported among Karachi residents who had no history of foreign travel. The department has stepped up surveillance, contact tracing, and patient care, emphasizing the importance of early testing, isolation, and strict infection prevention measures in healthcare facilities. Authorities have also advised the public to maintain proper hand hygiene and avoid direct contact with rashes, blisters, or sores on suspected or confirmed patients. Citizens are urged to seek immediate medical attention if they develop unusual rashes or blisters and to inform their doctors about any contact with a suspected monkeypox patient. The health department reiterated that monkeypox is a preventable and treatable public health concern, urging reliance on official sources for verified information.

news.source_body_en: The Sindh Health Department reported two additional monkeypox cases on October 24, 2026, bringing the provincial total to 98. This marks an intensification of the outbreak, with cases now being reported among Karachi residents who had no history of foreign travel. The department has stepped up surveillance, contact tracing, and patient care, emphasizing the importance of early testing, isolation, and strict infection prevention measures in healthcare facilities. Authorities have also advised the public to maintain proper hand hygiene and avoid direct contact with rashes, blisters, or sores on suspected or confirmed patients. Citizens are urged to seek immediate medical attention if they develop unusual rashes or blisters and to inform their doctors about any contact with a suspected monkeypox patient. The health department reiterated that monkeypox is a preventable and treatable public health concern, urging reliance on official sources for verified information.
news.content_zh: 信德省卫生部门于 2026 年 10 月 24 日报告了另外两例猴痘病例,使全省总数达到 98 例。这标志着 暴发 的加剧,目前报告的病例发生在没有出国旅行史的卡拉奇居民中。该部门加强了 监测、接触者追踪和患者护理,强调医疗机构中早期检测、隔离和严格感染预防措施的重要性。当局还建议公众保持适当的手部卫生,避免直接接触疑似或确诊患者的皮疹、水泡或疮口。敦促公民如果出现异常皮疹或水泡,请立即就医,并告知医生与疑似猴痘患者的任何接触。卫生部门重申,猴痘是一个可预防和可治疗的公共卫生问题,敦促依赖官方来源获取经过验证的信息。

PHOTO: PIXABAY KARACHI: One more child has died of mpox in Sindh, raising the province's death toll from the viral disease to 12 this year, as health authorities intensified surveillance, contact tracing and treatment measures following seven new cases reported over the past week. The total number of confirmed mpox cases in Sindh has reached 98, prompting the provincial health department to direct public and private hospitals to strictly implement infection prevention and control protocols to contain the spread of the virus. news.source_body_en: A child has died of mpox in Sindh, Pakistan, raising the province's death toll to 12 this year. The death was confirmed by a spokesperson from the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital at NIPA, who stated the child had been transferred from a private hospital a few days earlier. Health authorities have intensified surveillance, contact tracing, and treatment measures following seven new mpox cases reported over the past week. The total number of confirmed mpox cases in Sindh has reached 98. The virus is contagious and spreads through close physical contact, particularly via skin rashes, blisters, lesions, and contaminated personal belongings. Vulnerable groups include infants, individuals with weak immune systems, and those with other serious medical conditions. Authorities emphasize the importance of early diagnosis, isolation of infected patients, and strict adherence to medical guidelines to prevent further transmission. The report is based on a full original article published by The Express Tribune on October 25, 2026.

news.content: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages September 26, 2026 - October 25, 2026 GO Home Taiwan News Thu, Oct 22, 2026 page4 Mpox cases hit two-year high, CDC data show By Lee I-chia / Staff reporter Add TT as Preferred Source As of Monday, 18 new cases of mpox had been reported this month, topping the highest monthly number in two years, with local cases having been reported weekly for seven consecutive weeks, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said on Tuesday. CDC data showed that 52 mpox cases had been reported so far this year as of Monday, comprising 41 locally acquired cases and 11 imported. CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Director Guo Hung-wei (郭宏偉) said 18 cases were reported in the first 19 days of this month alone, including 16 with the Clade 1b mpox virus, a variant first identified in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in September 2023. Centers for Disease Control Deputy Director-General and spokesman Lin Min-cheng speaks at a news conference in Taipei in an undated photograph. Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times Contact tracing showed that the 16 cases were aged between 20 and 50, with all of them having had unsafe sex and only two having received an mpox vaccine, Guo said. Thirty people have tested positive for Clade 1b mpox so far this year, with 22 local cases and eight imported — six from Thailand and two from Hong Kong, he said. The risk of cross-border Clade 1b mpox viral transmission is increasing, with 68 countries and areas having reported confirmed cases, while mpox cases have been rising in parts of the WHO’s Western Pacific Region, Guo said. A WHO assessment report published in August showed that overall global public health risk is “moderate” for “individuals with multiple sexual partners,” and “low” for all other individuals, he said. CDC Deputy Director-General and spokesman Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said that local mpox cases have been reported weekly for seven consecutive weeks. The 52 local mpox cases reported so far this year is about 20 percent higher than the same period last year, Lin said. “We continue to urge people who are eligible for [mpox] vaccination to get fully vaccinated with two doses for full protection,” he said. Vaccination is the most effective method of preventing mpox infection, the CDC said, adding that getting the full two-dose regimen provides about 90 percent protection, while one dose provides about 40 to 80 percent. There are 327 healthcare facilities across Taiwan that provide publicly funded mpox vaccinations, so people who have engaged in high-risk sexual behavior, such as having multiple sexual partners, engaged in sex work or had sex at commercial venues should get vaccinated, it said. However, due to the weakening of a Pacific high-pressure system the storm is now expected to turn northward earlier than initially forecast, likely around Japan’s Ishigaki Island, Cheng said. elements_en.event: Mpox cases in Taiwan have reached a two-year high, with 18 new cases reported this month and local cases reported weekly for seven consecutive weeks. elements_en.scale_impact_and_risk: As of Monday, 18 new mpox cases were reported this month, with 52 cases in total this year. elements_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC is conducting contact tracing and urging eligible individuals to get vaccinated. The CDC also emphasized that people who have engaged in high-risk sexual behavior should consider vaccination.

news.source_body_en: The Taipei Times reported that mpox cases in Taiwan have reached a two-year high, with 18 new cases reported this month as of Monday, according to CDC data. Local cases have been reported weekly for seven consecutive weeks, and a total of 52 cases were recorded this year, comprising 41 locally acquired and 11 imported. The CDC highlighted that 16 of the 18 cases were linked to unsafe sex, with only two having received the mpox vaccine. The risk of cross-border transmission of Clade 1b mpox is increasing, as 68 countries and areas have confirmed cases. The WHO assessment report from August indicated a moderate global public health risk for individuals with multiple sexual partners. The CDC urged eligible individuals to get vaccinated, noting that the full two-dose regimen provides about 90 percent protection, while one dose offers 40 to 80 percent. The agency also emphasized that people engaging in high-risk sexual behavior should consider vaccination to prevent mpox infection.

news.content: TODAY’S PAPER | October 26, 2026 | EPAPER ☰ Home Latest Pakistan Business World Sports Opinion Life & Style T-Magazine Blogs Tech Cartoon Home Pakistan Mpox claims another child's life in Sindh, this year's death toll rises to 12 The child, a resident of Karachi, died during treatment at the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital in NIPA Faran Khan October 24, 2026 2 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email A laboratory nurse, takes a sample from a child declared a suspected case of mpox. Photo: Reuters KARACHI: Another child died of mpox in Karachi on Saturday, taking the number of deaths caused by the viral infection in Sindh this year to 12, as health authorities reported seven new cases over the past week and intensified surveillance, contact tracing, and treatment measures. According to Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital spokesperson Rashid Khan, the child, a resident of Karachi, was being treated in the hospital in NIPA for monkeypox and passed away during treatment, further revealed that the patient had been transferred to the facility from a private hospital a few days earlier. Khan said the total number of mpox cases reported in Sindh has climbed to 98. The Express Tribune contacted Sindh Institute of Skin Diseases (Regal) Additional Director and consultant dermatologist Dr Abdullah Yahya to learn about the disease. Read: Sindh reports two more monkeypox cases, tally rises to 98 Dr Yahya cautioned that mpox was a contagious viral disease that could spread through close physical contact with an infected person, including direct contact with skin lesions, blisters and sores. Advertisement X “The virus could also be transmitted through contaminated clothing, towels, bedding and other personal belongings used by an infected person,” he said, while stressing the need to avoid contact with contaminated items and affected persons. Dr Yahya also emphasised the importance of early diagnosis, isolating infected individuals and following medical advice to prevent further transmission. “Mpox can affect both children and adults, although the severity of the illness varies from person to person. Infants, people with weakened immune systems and those suffering from other underlying medical conditions may face a higher risk of severe illness and complications,” the skin doctor outlined. He also underscored the common symptoms of the virus, saying it includes fever, body aches, swollen lymph nodes, and unusual skin rashes, blisters or sores. According to Dr Yahya, suspected and confirmed patients should be kept separate under medical supervision, with appropriate infection-prevention measures in place. Most patients can recover with appropriate medical care and monitoring, he said, adding that immediate medical attention was necessary if severe symptoms developed. Karachi reports highest number of cases According to figures available with the provincial health department, Karachi has recorded the highest number of mpox cases in Sindh, with 26 infections reported. Khairpur has reported 22 cases, followed by Sukkur with nine and Hyderabad with five. Ghotki, Kashmore and Shaheed Benazirabad have recorded three cases each. Hospital sealed over infection-control concerns Separately, the Sindh Healthcare Commission has sealed Ibn-e-Hasan Hospital in Malir 15, Karachi, following concerns over infection-prevention arrangements after a laboratory report confirmed mpox in a 20-day-old newborn. According to information available to The Express Tribune, the infant had undergone circumcision at the hospital. The case has raised concerns about the implementation of infection-control protocols at healthcare facilities, particularly the sterilisation of medical instruments and the use of proper sterile procedures during treatment. Health authorities have stepped up efforts to identify and monitor close contacts of infected patients to prevent further spread of the virus. Patients being treated at government hospitals are being provided with medical care, while public and private healthcare facilities have been directed to follow prescribed infection-prevention measures and use appropriate protective equipment when examining and treating suspected cases. Dr Yahya also emphasised the importance of early diagnosis, isolating infected individuals and following medical advice to prevent further transmission. “Mpox can affect both children and adults, although the severity of the illness varies from person to person. Infants, people with weakened immune systems and those suffering from other underlying medical conditions may face a higher risk of severe illness and complications,” the skin doctor outlined. He also underscored the common symptoms of the virus, saying it includes fever, body aches, swollen lymph nodes, and unusual skin rashes, blisters or sores. According to Dr Yahya, suspected and confirmed patients should be kept separate under medical supervision, with appropriate infection-prevention measures in place. Most patients can recover with appropriate medical care and monitoring, he said, adding that immediate medical attention was necessary if severe symptoms developed. Karachi reports highest number of cases According to figures available with the provincial health department, Karachi has recorded the highest number of mpox cases in Sindh, with 26 infections reported. Health authorities have stepped up efforts to identify and monitor close contacts of infected patients to prevent further spread of the virus. October 25, 2026 Pakistan Saudi Arabia Middle East World Business Opinion Lifestyle Sport Latest News/Pakistan Pakistan says 2 soldiers, 6 militants killed during counterterror operation in northwest Home Infant dies of mpox in Pakistan’s Sindh, taking 2027 tally to 12 Infant dies of mpox in Pakistan’s Sindh, taking 2027 tally to 12 A poster indicating an isolation ward, prepared for mpox patients, is seen at the Police and Services hospital in Peshawar on August 20, 2024. (AFP/File) Short Url https://arab.news/jsu85 Infant contracted infection after undergoing circumcision at illegal hospital in Karachi, says health official Experts warn of local transmission as health records show 19 cases reported between late September to October Updated 24 October 2026 Arab News Pakistan October 24, 2026 10:55 KARACHI: A 53-day-old infant died in Pakistan’s Karachi city on Saturday after contracting monkeypox (mpox) disease, health officials said, raising this year’s death toll from the infection in the southern Sindh province to 12. The infant, a resident of Karachi’s Malir district, underwent a circumcision procedure at the Ibn-e-Hassan hospital in when he was 20 days old and developed symptoms four days later, according to health officials. He was subsequently transferred to the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital and Research Center (SIDH&RC) at Karachi’s NIPA area, where he died on Saturday, the hospital’s medical superintendent Dr. Abdul Wahid Rajput told Arab News. Mpox virus can spread to humans from an animal host, such as rodents or non-human primates like monkeys, and from humans themselves. A person infected with mpox suffers from flu-like symptoms and an itchy, painful rash. While historically localized to parts of Africa, a global outbreak in 2022 led to a surge in cases worldwide. “The child was 53 days old and had been transferred to our hospital from a private health care facility. The cause of death was mpox,” Dr. Rajput told Arab News. The Sindh Healthcare Commission (SHCC) said it has sealed Ibn-e-Hassan hospital in Karachi’s Malir after receiving a report from a district health officer confirming the infant contracted the disease from there. According to the commission, the child contracted mpox after circumcision was performed using contaminated scissors at the facility. It said a sample tested at a laboratory returned positive for the virus. The commission said its inspection found that the hospital was operating illegally, with unqualified staff and inadequate infection prevention and control measures in place. “The action was taken over poor hygiene, inadequate infection prevention and control measures, and reported malpractices that raised serious concerns about patient safety and public health,” the SHCC said in a statement shared with Arab News. The death comes amid concerns over local transmission of mpox in Sindh. Health department surveillance records obtained by Arab News show that 19 mpox cases were reported between late September and October in the province, including infections linked to close contact, family gatherings and suspected exposures at health care facilities. Sindh has recorded 98 mpox cases and 12 deaths so far this year, according to official data. The 19 reported mpox cases documented by the provincial health department from September to October include 12 patients from Karachi and seven from other districts in Sindh, with several investigations identifying contact between infected individuals. The records include infections that linked patients in Karachi’s Malir district and elsewhere in the province, suggesting that transmission is occurring through local contact. Seventeen of the 19 patients had no recorded travel history during the preceding 21 days, although the absence of travel does not independently establish where an infection was acquired. ’EXTREMELY DANGEROUS’ Dr. Rana Jawad Asghar, a Pakistani physician and epidemiologist, said the available information indicated local transmission. However, he said the extent of the outbreak remained difficult to determine without comprehensive epidemiological investigations. “Local transmission has either begun or is already taking place,” Dr. Asghar told Arab News. He said detailed investigations of most cases were not publicly available, making it difficult to establish whether infections were spreading within households, social networks or other settings. “Every mpox case needs to be investigated, contacts traced and links between cases mapped,” he said. Asghar called for stronger disease surveillance, outbreak investigations and contact tracing, saying the infection could still be contained through timely public health interventions. He also expressed serious concern over the reported infection involving surgical instruments, warning that inadequate infection-control practices could turn health care facilities into sources of disease transmission. “If a child contracted the infection through a surgical instrument, that is extremely dangerous,” he said. Asghar pointed to previous health care-associated infections involving children in Sindh and called for strict enforcement of infection prevention measures. “Hospitals must not become a source of disease transmission,” he said. “People should not go to hospitals for treatment and return with new infections.” Asghar said stronger surveillance, thorough case investigations and contact tracing remained essential to preventing further infections. “The outbreak is still at a stage where much can be done,” he said. (AFP/File) Short Url https://arab.news/jsu85 Infant contracted infection after undergoing circumcision at illegal hospital in Karachi, says health official Experts warn of local transmission as health records show 19 cases reported between late September to October Updated 24 October 2026 Arab News Pakistan October 24, 2026 10:55 KARACHI: A 53-day-old infant died in Pakistan’s Karachi city on Saturday after contracting monkeypox (mpox) disease, health officials said, raising this year’s death toll from the infection in the southern Sindh province to 12. The infant, a resident of Karachi’s Malir district, underwent a circumcision procedure at the Ibn-e-Hassan hospital in when he was 20 days old and developed symptoms four days later, according to health officials. He was subsequently transferred to the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital and Research Center (SIDH&RC) at Karachi’s NIPA area, where he died on Saturday, the hospital’s medical superintendent Dr. Abdul Wahid Rajput told Arab News. Mpox virus can spread to humans from an animal host, such as rodents or non-human primates like monkeys, and from humans themselves. A person infected with mpox suffers from flu-like symptoms and an itchy, painful rash. While historically localized to parts of Africa, a global outbreak in 2022 led to a surge in cases worldwide. “The child was 53 days old and had been transferred to our hospital from a private health care facility. The cause of death was mpox,” Dr. Rajput told Arab News. The Sindh Healthcare Commission (SHCC) said it has sealed Ibn-e-Hassan hospital in Karachi’s Malir after receiving a report from a district health officer confirming the infant contracted the disease from there. According to the commission, the child contracted mpox after circumcision was performed using contaminated scissors at the facility. It said a sample tested at a laboratory returned positive for the virus. The commission said its inspection found that the hospital was operating illegally, with unqualified staff and inadequate infection prevention and control measures in place. “The action was taken over poor hygiene, inadequate infection prevention and control measures, and reported malpractices that raised serious concerns about patient safety and public health,” the SHCC said in a statement shared with Arab News. The death comes amid concerns over local transmission of mpox in Sindh. Health department surveillance records obtained by Arab News show that 19 mpox cases were reported between late September and October in the province, including infections linked to close contact, family gatherings and suspected exposures at health care facilities. Sindh has recorded 98 mpox cases and 12 deaths so far this year, according to official data. The 19 reported mpox cases documented by the provincial health department from September to October include 12 patients from Karachi and seven from other districts in Sindh, with several investigations identifying contact between infected individuals. The records include infections that linked patients in Karachi’s Malir district and elsewhere in the province, suggesting that transmission is occurring through local contact. Seventeen of the 19 patients had no recorded travel history during the preceding 21 days, although the absence of travel does not independently establish where an infection was acquired. ’EXTREMELY DANGEROUS’ Dr. Rana Jawad Asghar, a Pakistani physician and epidemiologist, said the available information indicated local transmission. However, he said the extent of the outbreak remained difficult to determine without comprehensive epidemiological investigations. “Local transmission has either begun or is already taking place,” Dr. Asghar told Arab News. He said detailed investigations of most cases were not publicly available, making it difficult to establish whether infections were spreading within households, social networks or other settings. “Every mpox case needs to be investigated, contacts traced and links between cases mapped,” he said. Asghar called for stronger disease surveillance, outbreak investigations and contact tracing, saying the infection could still be contained through timely public health interventions. He also expressed serious concern over the reported infection involving surgical instruments, warning that inadequate infection-control practices could turn health care facilities into sources of disease transmission. “If a child contracted the infection through a surgical instrument, that is extremely dangerous,” he said. Asghar pointed to previous health care-associated infections involving children in Sindh and called for strict enforcement of infection prevention measures. “Hospitals must not become a source of disease transmission,” he said. “People should not go to hospitals for treatment and return with new infections.” Asghar said stronger surveillance, thorough case investigations and contact tracing remained essential to preventing further infections. “The outbreak is still at a stage where much can be done,” he said. news.content: News Health Taiwan reports highest number of mpox cases in October in two years — Taipei Times Fedir Kryshtovskyi 22 October 2026 02:53 Taiwan recorded 18 mpox cases in the first 19 days of October, the highest monthly figure in the past two years. Local infection cases have been reported every week for seven consecutive weeks, Taipei Times reports , citing Taiwan’s Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Since the beginning of the year, as of Monday, Taiwan has recorded 52 mpox cases: 41 infections were detected within the country, while another 11 cases were imported. According to Guo Hongwei, director of the Center for Epidemic Intelligence, 16 of the 18 cases registered in October involved the Clade 1b virus variant, which was first identified in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in September 2023. Clade 1b cases In total, 30 people have tested positive for Clade 1b this year. Of these, 22 cases were local and eight were imported: six from Thailand and two from Hong Kong. According to contact tracing data, the 16 people with Clade 1b registered in October were between 20 and 50 years old, all had unprotected sexual contact, and only two had received an mpox vaccination. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Guo Hongwei said that the risk of cross-border spread of Clade 1b is growing, as confirmed cases of this variant have been recorded in 68 countries and territories. He also drew attention to an increase in mpox cases in some countries of the WHO Western Pacific Region. Vaccination recommendations Taiwan’s CDC said that the number of cases recorded this year is about 20% higher than during the same period last year. The agency urged people eligible for vaccination to complete the two-dose vaccine course. According to the CDC’s estimate, full vaccination provides about 90% protection, while one dose provides from 40% to 80%. State-funded mpox vaccination in Taiwan is available at 327 medical institutions. The CDC urged vaccination for people who had sexual contact with multiple partners, engaged in sex work, or had sex at commercial venues. Read us on Download our app

news.content_original: News Health Taiwan reports highest number of mpox cases in October in two years — Taipei Times Fedir Kryshtovskyi 22 October 2026 02:53 Taiwan recorded 18 mpox cases in the first 19 days of October, the highest monthly figure in the past two years. Local infection cases have been reported every week for seven consecutive weeks, Taipei Times reports , citing Taiwan’s Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Since the beginning of the year, as of Monday, Taiwan has recorded 52 mpox cases: 41 infections were detected within the country, while another 11 cases were imported. According to Guo Hongwei, director of the Center for Epidemic Intelligence, 16 of the 18 cases registered in October involved the Clade 1b virus variant, which was first identified in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in September 2023. Clade 1b cases In total, 30 people have tested positive for Clade 1b this year. Of these, 22 cases were local and eight were imported: six from Thailand and two from Hong Kong. According to contact tracing data, the 16 people with Clade 1b registered in October were between 20 and 50 years old, all had unprotected sexual contact, and only two had received an mpox vaccination. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Guo Hongwei said that the risk of cross-border spread of Clade 1b is growing, as confirmed cases of this variant have been recorded in 68 countries and territories. He also drew attention to an increase in mpox cases in some countries of the WHO Western Pacific Region. Vaccination recommendations Taiwan’s CDC said that the number of cases recorded this year is about 20% higher than during the same period last year. The agency urged people eligible for vaccination to complete the two-dose vaccine course. According to the CDC’s estimate, full vaccination provides about 90% protection, while one dose provides from 40% to 80%. State-funded mpox vaccination in Taiwan is available at 327 medical institutions. The CDC urged vaccination for people who had sexual contact with multiple partners, engaged in sex work, or had sex at commercial venues. Read us on Download our app

news.content_title: Health District reports first Clade I mpox case in Clark County resident
news.content: LAS VEGAS (KLAS) -- The Southern Nevada Health District announced Tuesday the first confirmed case of clade I mpox in a Clark County resident. The district said the person has no reported travel exposure. >>Download the free 8 News+ app for live newscasts and streaming originals Additionally, the Health District reported 11 confirmed cases of clade II mpox since August 2026. This marks a recent increase in cases. "This first clade I case and the recent increase in clade II cases are reminders that mpox continues to circulate in our community," Dr. Cassius Lockett, District Health Officer for the Health District, said. "We encourage people at risk to get vaccinated and anyone who may have been exposed to seek guidance promptly. Recognizing symptoms and avoiding close contact when sick can also help prevent further spread." Mpox is caused by two types of the virus, which are known as clade I and clade II. Clade II is the type that caused the global outbreak that started in 2022. That outbreak continues to circulate at low levels in the United States, the health district release said. A large clade I outbreak has spread widely in Central and Eastern Africa since 2024, with cases also identified in other countries, such as the United States. Both types of the virus can be prevented in the same way, and the JYNNEOS is expected to protect against both. The Health District offers mpox vaccines for those over 18 who are eligible at immunization clinics. The vaccine is given in two doses, four weeks apart. Appointments are available at this link . Those who may have been exposed should contact a health care provider about a vaccine and monitor for any symptoms for 21 days after the last exposure. "Mpox spreads primarily through close, sustained physical contact, including sexual or intimate contact," the release said. "It can spread through direct contact with a person's rash, sores, scabs or bodily fluids, including during kissing or oral, anal or vaginal sex. It can also spread through contact with contaminated items, such as clothing, bedding or towels, and during pregnancy or childbirth." Symptoms can begin within three weeks of exposure and illness may last two to four weeks. A rash may appear as bumps or blisters on or near the genitals or anus, or on other areas such as the hands, feet, chest, face or mouth. Other symptoms can include fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, muscle aches, and fatigue. Some people develop a rash without other symptoms. People with suspected or confirmed mpox should take the following steps to prevent spreading the illness: Stay home and avoid close contact with others, including people and pets in the same household. Avoid sexual contact, kissing, and other close physical contact. If being around others is unavoidable, wear a well-fitting mask and completely cover rashes and sores with clothing or bandages. Avoid sharing clothing, bedding, towels and other personal items. Wash hands frequently with soap and water, especially after touching the rash. Use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer if soap and water are unavailable. People with mpox should continue isolation until all sores have healed, scabs have fallen off, and a fresh layer of skin has formed. news.content_original: LAS VEGAS (KLAS) -- The Southern Nevada Health District announced Tuesday the first confirmed case of clade I mpox in a Clark County resident. The district said the person has no reported travel exposure. >>Download the free 8 News+ app for live newscasts and streaming originals Additionally, the Health District reported 11 confirmed cases of clade II mpox since August 2026. This marks a recent increase in cases. "This first clade I case and the recent increase in clade II cases are reminders that mpox continues to circulate in our community," Dr. Cassius Lockett, District Health Officer for the Health District, said. "We encourage people at risk to get vaccinated and anyone who may have been exposed to seek guidance promptly. Recognizing symptoms and avoiding close contact when sick can also help prevent further spread." Mpox is caused by two types of the virus, which are known as clade I and clade II. Clade II is the type that caused the global outbreak that started in 2022. That outbreak continues to circulate at low levels in the United States, the health district release said. A large clade I outbreak has spread widely in Central and Eastern Africa since 2024, with cases also identified in other countries, such as the United States. Both types of the virus can be prevented in the same way, and the JYNNEOS is expected to protect against both. The Health District offers mpox vaccines for those over 18 who are eligible at immunization clinics. The vaccine is given in two doses, four weeks apart. Appointments are available at this link . Those who may have been exposed should contact a health care provider about a vaccine and monitor for any symptoms for 21 days after the last exposure. "Mpox spreads primarily through close, sustained physical contact, including sexual or intimate contact," the release said. "It can spread through direct contact with a person's rash, sores, scabs or bodily fluids, including during kissing or oral, anal or vaginal sex. It can also spread through contact with contaminated items, such as clothing, bedding or towels, and during pregnancy or childbirth." Symptoms can begin within three weeks of exposure and illness may last two to four weeks. A rash may appear as bumps or blisters on or near the genitals or anus, or on other areas such as the hands, feet, chest, face or mouth. Other symptoms can include fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, muscle aches, and fatigue. Some people develop a rash without other symptoms. People with suspected or confirmed mpox should take the following steps to prevent spreading the illness: Stay home and avoid close contact with others, including people and pets in the same household. Avoid sexual contact, kissing, and other close physical contact. If being around others is unavoidable, wear a well-fitting mask and completely cover rashes and sores with clothing or bandages. Avoid sharing clothing, bedding, towels and other personal items. Wash hands frequently with soap and water, especially after touching the rash. Use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer if soap and water are unavailable. People with mpox should continue isolation until all sores have healed, scabs have fallen off, and a fresh layer of skin has formed.
